by_component.description: Planned to become the sole provisioning path for the preproduction bench, applying the same signed baseline used for flight units so bench behaviour matches delivered behaviour.
Planned to be constrained by configuration and by procedure so that it cannot hold a session on the preproduction bench and an operational segment in the same connection state.

control_implementations.narrative: Operational mission data is occasionally needed on the WS-X90 preproduction bench to reproduce a fielded defect. Aurora plans two controls around it: a recorded, expiring approval that names the data set and the approving authority, held with the provisioning record on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017); and a handling rule that raises the bench and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) to the protection level of the flight Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) for as long as the approval is live, with sanitisation before the laptop returns to general support use. Today the approval is informal and the handling rule is unwritten. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to hold the live-data approval record alongside the bench provisioning record, and to expire the approval automatically at 90 days.
Planned to be handled at the flight protection level for the life of a live-data approval and sanitised to a recorded procedure before returning to general support use.
Sets the protection level the bench must match; its storage handling rules are the reference the bench rule is written against.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 navigation and timing hardware is the part of the platform with the shortest supplier production horizon, and Aurora has no dated refresh plan for it. The planned build is a refresh schedule holding, for the Timing Receiver (LRU-005), Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006), a replacement decision point tied to the vendor end-of-production date recorded against each item. Availability for WS-X90 is categorised moderate, so the schedule targets planned replacement inside the sustainment cycle rather than hot spare inventory. Nothing is scheduled today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to carry a dated replacement decision point tied to its vendor end-of-production date; the processor's integrity-check firmware is the item with the longest requalification lead time.
Planned to carry the earliest replacement decision point in the schedule, since its receiver front end has the shortest declared production horizon.
Planned to be refreshed with the sensor interface bus revision so that the interface and the processor are requalified as a pair rather than separately.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 LRU procurement packages carry the security functional and assurance requirements allocated to that LRU by control id drawn from the tailored profile, together with the acceptance criteria the first article must meet; the resulting acceptance record is filed against the LRU entry in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) inventory entry is not marked accepted until it exists. That path works for the LRUs procured after the tailoring baseline was set. It does not cover the three ground support items bought before it — their packages reference the superseded 74-control set, so the allocated requirements for the SA, SR and CM enhancements added by the re-derivation were never placed on contract and are being retrofitted through engineering change rather than acquisition. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds the procurement package, the allocated control ids and the first-article acceptance record for each LRU as linked configuration items.
Will not mark an inventory entry accepted until the matching first-article acceptance record exists in LRU-020, which is what makes the acquisition requirement observable on the platform.

control_implementations.narrative: The suppliers of the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) deliver a functional properties description for every security function exposed at the LRU boundary. Each description states the inputs the function accepts, the outputs and error states it can return, and the externally observable behaviour of every enforcement decision — including what an assessor sees when the function denies. The descriptions are held against the LRU record in the Configuration Repository and are what the assessment procedures for the boot and key-use controls are written from, so a change to an enforcement behaviour surfaces as a documentation delta before it surfaces as a test failure. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Supplier-delivered description covers key generation, key use and key release refusal, stating the observable output for each denial condition rather than only the success path.

Supplier-delivered description covers measurement, verification and halt behaviour, including which measurements are extended before control is passed and what an observer sees on a failed verification.

control_implementations.narrative: Security-relevant external interface specifications and high-level design are held for the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) at a depth that lets an assessor trace each enforcement decision back to a named interface rather than to a subsystem. LRU-003 and LRU-007 additionally have low-level design available for review under the supplier agreement. LRU-011 does not: the interlock supplier has delivered the interface specification and a block-level design, but the low-level design covering the authorization state machine is still being negotiated, which leaves the independent-authorization argument resting on the supplier's assertion rather than on reviewed design. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Interface specification and low-level design available for review, letting each key-release decision be traced to the interface that requests it.
Interface specification and low-level design available for review, covering the policy decision point and the fail-closed path on the external boundary.
Interface specification and block-level design delivered; the low-level design for the authorization state machine is outstanding, so the interlock argument is not yet independently reviewable.

control_implementations.narrative: Aurora plans to require the mission software supplier to demonstrate the development life cycle actually used for the release that ships, rather than the process described in the proposal — the systems engineering method, the security engineering method, and the verification and quality gates — evidenced against the build record for the Mission Computer (LRU-001) software held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). The demonstration is planned as a walkthrough at each qualification gate. No walkthrough has been held and the contractual hook does not yet exist. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Its mission software release is the subject of the planned life-cycle demonstration, since it is the largest supplier-developed item on the platform.
Holds the build record the demonstration is checked against, so the process described can be compared with the artefacts the process actually produced.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 LRUs are delivered with the approved hardened configuration already applied: the delivered configuration hash is compared with the approved baseline recorded in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) at first power-on and there is no post-delivery hardening step to forget. The Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) reapplies the same approved configuration as the default on reinstallation and recovery, so a recovered LRU comes up hardened rather than at vendor defaults. The gap is on the recovery side: the default-reapply path is verified for mission computing and platform management LRUs, but the payload interface LRUs recover to a supplier default profile that a technician must then correct by hand, which is exactly the manual step the control exists to remove. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds the approved delivery configuration and its hash for every LRU, and is the reference the first power-on comparison is made against.
Reapplies the approved delivery configuration as the default on every reinstallation and recovery; the payload interface path still falls back to a supplier default profile.

control_implementations.narrative: The commercial information assurance products inside the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) were selected on functional grounds; their evaluation status was not a selection criterion and is not recorded anywhere the program can query. Aurora plans to record, per product, either the NIAP Protection Profile it was evaluated against or — where no profile applies to the technology type and the product enforces its policy with cryptography — the FIPS 140 validation or NSA approval by certificate number. The register does not exist yet and two of the three product certificate positions are unknown. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Its commercial waveform security stack is the product with the least understood evaluation status; the planned register entry must establish whether an applicable protection profile exists at all.
Its commercial policy enforcement product is expected to carry an applicable protection profile evaluation; the planned register entry records the profile and evaluation identifier.
Enforces its security policy with cryptography, so its register entry must carry a module validation or approval certificate number rather than only a profile reference.

control_implementations.narrative: Each WS-X90 supplier declares the functions, ports, protocols and services its LRU uses in operational configuration, and that declaration is the set the platform permits: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) external rule set and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) segment policy are generated from the declarations rather than maintained by hand, and anything undeclared is denied by default. The Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) declaration is the tightest on the platform, listing a fixed set of sensor bus services with no management protocol exposed. A declaration change is a configuration change: the generated rule set is rebuilt and the delta is reviewed before the release ships. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: External rule set is generated from the supplier declarations; any flow not present in a declaration is denied by default and the denial is logged with the attempted service.
Internal segment policy is generated from the same declarations, so an LRU that starts using an undeclared internal service is blocked at the switch rather than discovered later.
Declares a fixed sensor bus service set with no management protocol exposed, which is what lets its segment policy be written as an allow-list of three services.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 has no PIV-based credential path. Technicians authenticate to the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) using the platform's own credential store, and no approved-products selection has been made for credential readers because no reader is fitted. Nothing is implemented against this control today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: No credential reader fitted and no approved-products selection made; technician authentication uses the platform credential store.
No credential reader fitted; the conditional maintenance endpoint authenticates through the same platform credential store.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 ships two documentation sets that are treated as configuration items rather than deliverable prose. The administrator set covers the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and Platform Management Controller (LRU-013): secure configuration and operation of every privileged maintenance function, the effective use of each security mechanism the technician touches, and the known configuration weaknesses a technician must avoid — reissued with each configuration baseline change so a technician never works from a set that predates the baseline on the unit. The operator set covers the mission software on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the payload health displays fed by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012), and describes each security function an operator can invoke together with the behaviour the system exhibits when that function denies an action, which is the part operators most often lack. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Administrator set covers every privileged maintenance function it exposes, including the session constraints and the known configuration weaknesses a technician must avoid.
Administrator set covers platform inventory and administrative service operation and is reissued whenever its configuration baseline changes.
Operator set describes the security functions the mission software exposes to the crew and the observable behaviour on denial.
Operator set describes how payload health and status indications are interpreted, including the indication shown when telemetry integrity cannot be confirmed.

control_implementations.narrative: The WS-X90 security architecture description names, per subsystem, the engineering principles applied and the specific design decision that carries each one — so a reviewer can follow a principle to a mechanism instead of to a statement of intent. The mission computing sections are written to that depth: least privilege resolves to the service manifest check on the Platform Management Controller, hierarchical trust resolves to the boot measurement chain, and mediated access resolves to a named enforcement point. The Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) sections are equally complete. What is missing is the same treatment for the navigation and timing subsystem and for the payload interface: the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) sections still assert principles without naming the design decision that carries them, which is the failure mode the control exists to prevent. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Architecture sections trace each applied principle to a named mission computing mechanism — service manifest enforcement, domain separation and the mediation point for payload command authority.
Architecture sections trace trusted components and hierarchical trust to the key release precondition and the measurement the module checks before releasing key material.
Architecture sections currently assert the principles without naming the design decisions that carry them; the interlock write-up is the outstanding item for this control.

control_implementations.narrative: Mission applications on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) reach payload command authority today through a thin wrapper over the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) register map, which means the abstraction leaks: an application that knows the register layout can compose a command the wrapper never intended. The planned change presents payload command authority as a single named abstraction with one entry point and no register-level alternative, so that the mediation the interface controller performs cannot be bypassed by an application that understands the hardware. The abstraction is specified but not yet built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to lose direct register access to the payload path; mission applications will hold only the single command-authority abstraction.
Planned to expose one entry point for payload command authority and to reject register-level writes that do not arrive through it.

control_implementations.narrative: Mission applications at different trust levels on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) currently share one message-passing mechanism and one switch queue, so a fault or a flood in a low-trust application is felt by a high-trust one. The planned separation gives each trust level its own queue with its own quota on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) VLAN, removing the shared mechanism that would otherwise be a common path between them. The queue split is designed; the switch quota configuration has not been written. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to run one message queue per trust level rather than a shared broker, so an application cannot influence a higher-trust peer through queue occupancy.
Planned to carry a per-trust-level VLAN with an enforced quota, so contention stays inside a trust level.

control_implementations.narrative: The Mission Computer (LRU-001) is built in declared layers with the security enforcement services below the mission applications and no upward calls, and that layering is documented and reviewed. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004) is the incomplete half: navigation integrity checking is being separated into its own loadable module with a declared interface so a sensor fusion change cannot alter the integrity check without a separate signed module release, but the current build still compiles fusion and integrity checking into one image, so the separation exists on paper and not in the delivered firmware. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Integrity checking is specified as a separately loadable module with a declared interface; the shipped firmware still builds it into the sensor fusion image, which is the outstanding work.
Runs the declared layering today — enforcement services sit below mission applications with no upward calls, and the layer map is reviewed at each release.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 initialisation is currently ordered by convention rather than by a declared dependency graph, and one circularity is known: a platform service consumed by the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) itself waits on navigation data during a cold start. The planned change makes initialisation a directed acyclic graph with the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) completing before any service it protects, and removes the navigation circularity by giving the sensor interface a boot-time default that does not require navigation. The graph is drawn; the boot sequence has not been changed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to be the declared root of the initialisation graph, completing measurement before any protected service is permitted to start.
Planned to start from a boot-time default that has no dependency on navigation data, removing the known circular wait at cold start.

control_implementations.narrative: Payload command mediation should happen once, at the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010), and it should be cheap enough that no mission application on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) has an incentive to look for a faster path around it. The planned design fixes a mediation budget of 5 ms on the command path so that mediation is not the reason a developer proposes a bypass. The budget is set in the interface specification; the mediation path has not been measured against it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to perform payload command mediation once, on the command path, inside a 5 ms budget measured at the interface.
Planned to have no alternative payload command path, so the mediated route is also the only route and the fastest available.

control_implementations.narrative: The Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) and Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) both use pooled buffers, and a buffer released by one security domain can today be handed to another without being cleared. The planned change removes the sharing: buffers are partitioned per domain, and any buffer that does cross a domain boundary is zeroised before reuse. The partitioning is specified for both LRUs and neither has shipped it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to partition sensor input buffers per security domain and to zeroise any buffer that crosses a domain boundary before it is reused.
Planned to apply the same partitioning to telemetry staging buffers, so payload health data cannot be recovered from a buffer released to another domain.

control_implementations.narrative: The Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) authorization path is the smallest security-critical body of code on WS-X90 and the program intends to keep it small enough to review in full: a bounded state machine, no dynamic memory allocation, and no more externally reachable entry points than the interface specification declares. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004) integrity path is held to the same rule. Neither has been through the review that would establish the bound, and the interlock currently allocates at initialisation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to hold the authorization path to a bounded state machine with no dynamic allocation and a declared, closed set of externally reachable entry points.
Planned to hold the navigation integrity path to the same complexity bound so it can be reviewed in full at each release.

control_implementations.narrative: The WS-X90 update format handled by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) has no explicit capability field, so adding a new security function to a future release means either changing the format for every LRU at once or accepting a weaker verification during the transition. The planned format carries an explicit version and capability field, letting a new function be introduced without relaxing verification of the current one, with the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) recording the capability set each release requires. The format revision is drafted and not yet fielded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to accept an update format carrying explicit version and capability fields and to refuse an image whose declared capability set exceeds what the LRU can verify.
Planned to record the capability set each release requires alongside the signed release metadata, so a mismatch is visible before staging.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 records, for each component another component depends on for a security decision, the basis on which that component is trusted — evaluation, review depth, and the enforcement it performs. The map is complete for mission computing: the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) trustworthiness basis is the hardware root of trust and its reviewed verification path, and the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) basis is its module validation plus the reviewed key release precondition. The Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) is the gap: it is depended on for an authorization decision but its supplier assurance case has not been delivered, so the rule that it must not accept an authorization from a component with a weaker basis cannot yet be evaluated. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Depended on for payload authorization, but its supplier assurance case is undelivered, so its trustworthiness basis is asserted rather than established.
Trustworthiness basis is recorded as the hardware root of trust plus the reviewed verification path, and is the anchor other bases are compared against.
Trustworthiness basis is recorded as the validated module plus the reviewed key release precondition, and it refuses callers whose basis is not recorded.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 platform trust is rooted in the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) hardware root of trust, and the intended rule is that nothing is trusted by something below it in the boot chain — in particular the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) should refuse to release key material to a caller whose boot measurement is absent. Today the module releases keys on a caller identity check alone, so the hierarchy is asserted by the boot design but not enforced at the key boundary. The measurement precondition is specified for the next module firmware release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Establishes the platform measurement chain that the trust hierarchy is rooted in; already produces the measurement the key boundary will consume.
Planned to add a boot measurement precondition to key release, so a caller with no recorded measurement is refused rather than accepted on identity alone.

control_implementations.narrative: Modification of the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) currently requires the same signing authority as a mission application update, so the components carrying the most platform trust are no harder to change than the ones carrying the least. No graded modification authority exists and none has been designed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Modification currently requires the same authority as any other signed image; no elevated authorisation is enforced.
Modification of stored security material follows the same single signing authority as ordinary configuration changes.

control_implementations.narrative: Mission applications on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) presently obtain some protected services from peers at their own trust level, which means a higher-trust function can depend on a lower-trust provider. The planned rule is that a component obtains protection only from a component at or above its own trust level, and that the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) — the highest-trust element in the payload path — depends on nothing below it. The service placement change is designed and not yet applied. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to obtain protected services only from components at or above the requesting application's trust level, removing the peer-provided cases in the current build.
Planned to hold no dependency on a lower-trust component for any part of its authorization decision.

control_implementations.narrative: The set of WS-X90 elements that must be trusted for a payload command to be authorised is intended to be exactly two — the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) and the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) — with any addition to that set requiring an architecture change decision rather than a code review. Today the set is three, because the payload interface controller also holds a residual authorization check inherited from an earlier design. Removing it is planned for the next payload firmware release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Intended to be one of only two elements that must be trusted for payload command authorization, holding the interlock decision itself.
Intended to be the other, holding the key use that binds the authorization to a verified origin.

control_implementations.narrative: Every WS-X90 platform service runs with the narrowest privilege set that lets it complete its function, and the rule is enforced rather than reviewed: each service ships with a manifest declaring the privileges it needs, the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) compares that manifest against the approved baseline at service start and refuses to launch a service requesting a privilege the baseline does not grant, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) applies the same check to technician sessions so a maintenance session cannot acquire a privilege beyond the one its task declares. Mission applications on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) run under the same manifest mechanism. Refusals are logged with the requested privilege, which is what makes privilege creep visible in the platform log rather than at the next review. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Compares each service manifest against the approved baseline at start and refuses to launch a service requesting an undeclared privilege, logging the refusal with the privilege requested.
Applies the same manifest check to technician maintenance sessions, so a session cannot hold a privilege beyond the one its declared task requires.
Hosts mission applications under the manifest mechanism, so an application's privilege set is fixed by its approved manifest rather than by what it asks for at runtime.

control_implementations.narrative: Payload release on WS-X90 is authorised by a single authority today. Two-authority concurrence at the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) has been raised as a design option and rejected for the current build on schedule grounds; no dual-authority mechanism exists in the interlock or in the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010). This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Opens the interlock on a single authorization today; no second-authority input is wired or implemented.
Carries one authorization credential on the command path with no provision for a second independent one.

control_implementations.narrative: The Timing Receiver (LRU-005) currently passes an external timing solution through with a quality flag, which makes the platform's timing trustworthiness a function of the external source's continued correctness. The planned behaviour makes the receiver self-reliant: on loss of the external reference, or on disagreement between the reference and the internal holdover beyond the declared tolerance, it enters holdover and marks its output degraded rather than passing unvalidated time to the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) and the platform log. The holdover discipline is specified and the disagreement threshold is agreed; the firmware change is not built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to enter holdover and mark its output degraded on loss of, or disagreement with, the external reference rather than passing unvalidated time through.
Consumes platform time for measurement records and is planned to treat a degraded timing indication as a distinct state rather than as valid time.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 composes with external mission systems across the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) boundary, and no analysis has been performed of the security policy that results from that composition — each side's policy is documented, the composed policy is not. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Enforces the WS-X90 side of the external boundary; the policy that results from composing it with the external system's policy has not been analysed.
Carries the internal side of the composition; no composed-policy statement covers the internal segment boundary.

control_implementations.narrative: Channels on WS-X90 are authenticated before they carry anything. Across the platform boundary, the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) wired path and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) mission link both complete mutual authentication using key material held in the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and fail closed if authentication does not complete — there is no unauthenticated fallback and no plaintext bypass for degraded operation. Internally, traffic between the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) and the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) runs on a channel bound to the LRU identity established at boot, so a substituted or spoofed LRU cannot present itself as the payload interface even from inside the airframe. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Completes mutual authentication on every external wired connection and fails closed when it does not complete; holds no unauthenticated fallback path.
Completes mutual authentication on the mission link before carrying mission data, using key material it never holds in the clear.
Holds the key material for both external channels and performs the key use, so channel authentication cannot be satisfied without it.
Carries the internal payload channel bound to the LRU identity, refusing to forward payload traffic from an unbound port.
Presents the boot-established LRU identity on the internal channel, so a substituted interface controller cannot take over the payload path.

control_implementations.narrative: Protection of stored security material on WS-X90 is continuous across power state changes for the mission computing path: the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) exposes no plaintext at any point in the boot sequence before the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) has established the platform integrity state, and a cold start that fails verification leaves the material sealed. The gap is the payload interface cold start, which uses a separate power domain that comes up before the platform integrity state is established; the material it reads is not sensitive today, but the sequence means the property cannot be claimed platform-wide. Resequencing the payload domain is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Keeps stored security material sealed until the platform integrity state is established, exposing no plaintext during the boot sequence on the mission computing path.
Establishes the integrity state that the storage module's unseal is conditioned on, and halts before unseal if verification fails.

control_implementations.narrative: Telemetry produced by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) is protected in transit, but its metadata — labels, timestamps and source identifiers — is carried in the clear alongside it, which leaks payload activity patterns to anything that can observe the export path even when the payload content is protected. The planned change protects metadata to the same level as the telemetry content on the path to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), including binding the source identifier so it cannot be rewritten in transit. The change is specified and not built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to protect telemetry labels, timestamps and source identifiers to the same level as the telemetry content, and to bind the source identifier against rewriting.
Planned to reject exported telemetry whose metadata binding does not verify, rather than accepting the record and trusting the label.

control_implementations.narrative: Neither the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) nor the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) currently checks its own integrity-check function; a fault that disabled the check would present as a stream of passing results. The planned behaviour has each run a self-check of its own checking function at least once per mission phase and report the outcome to the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), so a silent failure of the check becomes an observable absence of a report. The self-check design is agreed and unbuilt. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to run a periodic self-check of its navigation integrity-check function and report the outcome, so a disabled check is distinguishable from a passing one.
Planned to run the equivalent self-check of its holdover monitoring, reporting on the same cadence.
Planned to treat a missing self-check report as a fault condition rather than as an absence of news, raising it on the platform health view.

control_implementations.narrative: Security-relevant actions on WS-X90 are attributable to an identified actor and traceable to the component that performed them, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) resolves component identity from the record rather than inferring it from the source address. The Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) has been changed to stamp its records with a resolvable identity and that build is fielded. The collector side is not finished: its identity resolution table has not been populated for payload sources, so LRU-012 records currently resolve to a subsystem rather than to the unit, and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) retains the records at full fidelity meanwhile so the trace can be completed retrospectively once the table lands. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Stamps each exported record with an identity the collector can resolve without inference; the fielded build carries the change.
Resolves component identity from the record rather than the transport, but its resolution table is not yet populated for payload sources, so payload records resolve only to subsystem level.
Retains the unresolved records at full fidelity so the attribution can be completed once the resolution table is populated.

control_implementations.narrative: Configurable security options on WS-X90 ship in their restrictive state, and the rule is enforced at intake: a baseline entering the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with a permissive default is rejected, and the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) restores the restrictive state on recovery so a recovered unit is not more permissive than a delivered one. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) reports any runtime deviation from the restrictive default. Coverage is not complete: the intake check runs against mission computing and platform management baselines but not against ground support tooling baselines, so a permissive default in the provisioning toolchain would pass intake unnoticed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Rejects at intake any baseline whose configurable security options are not in their restrictive state; the check does not yet run against ground support tooling baselines.
Restores the restrictive default state during recovery so a recovered unit is never more permissive than a delivered one.
Reports runtime deviation from the restrictive default on the platform health view, which is how a manual relaxation becomes visible.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 fails into a state that grants no capability rather than into a permissive one. The Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) halts on a failed integrity check without passing control, and that behaviour is verified. The Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) is designed to remain closed through a failure rather than defaulting open, but the fail-closed test has not been run on the fielded interlock build, so the behaviour is designed and not demonstrated. On the recovery side, the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) restores from a signed image held in the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and stops rather than proceeding when it cannot verify the source; that path is verified for mission computing and has not been exercised for the payload interface. Availability for WS-X90 is moderate, so recovery is a controlled, attended action rather than an automatic failover. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Halts in a no-capability state on a failed integrity check; verified by test on the fielded build.
Designed to remain closed through a failure rather than defaulting open; the fail-closed test on the fielded build has not yet been run.
Stops rather than proceeding when it cannot verify the recovery source, and does not reduce the protection state to complete faster.
Holds the signed recovery images the controller restores from, so recovery does not depend on an off-platform source.

control_implementations.narrative: No analysis has been performed of the cost to an adversary of defeating a WS-X90 protection relative to the value of what it protects, and no protection has been selected or sized on that basis. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: No adversary-cost analysis exists for the mission computing protections it hosts.
No adversary-cost analysis exists for the platform management and inventory protections it provides.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 protections have not been assessed for their effect on mission performance, and no performance budget has been allocated to security functions on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) or the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) command path. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: No security performance budget allocated; the cost of enforcement services in the mission timeline is unmeasured.
No security performance budget allocated on the payload command path beyond the mediation figure proposed under the mediated-access work.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 maintenance and provisioning interfaces have not been reviewed for the errors a technician is likely to make under field conditions, and no human factors input has been taken on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) session flow or the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) tooling. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Session flow has not been reviewed for likely technician error; no confirmation or recovery affordances have been specified on that basis.
Support tooling has had no human factors review; error-prone steps are identified only from incident reports after the fact.

control_implementations.narrative: No assessment has been made of whether WS-X90 security controls are acceptable to the technicians and operators who must work with them, and no data exists on where the controls are being worked around in the field. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: No acceptability data collected on maintenance session constraints; workaround behaviour is unmeasured.
No acceptability data collected on the provisioning workflow, which is the longest-duration controlled procedure in ground support.

control_implementations.narrative: Provisioning a WS-X90 LRU is currently done from a written work instruction that leaves several steps to technician judgement, so two runs of the same provisioning can produce different recorded outcomes. The planned change makes provisioning a numbered procedure executed from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) whose steps produce the same recorded outcome on repetition, with each run writing a provisioning record to the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) that names the procedure revision it followed. The procedure is drafted and not yet in use. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to execute provisioning from a numbered procedure with no judgement steps, so repetition produces the same recorded outcome.
Planned to receive a provisioning record for every run, naming the procedure revision followed and the resulting configuration hash.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 ground support procedures apply the same ceremony regardless of what they touch, which makes the high-consequence ones no more rigorous than a read-only diagnostic and encourages technicians to treat all of them lightly. The planned change grades rigour by the trust of the component touched: a procedure that writes to the Secure Boot Controller requires two-person execution from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), while a read-only diagnostic from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) does not. The grading is drafted against the component trust levels and is not yet in the procedure set. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to require two-person execution for procedures that write to high-trust components, recorded against the provisioning run.
Planned to run read-only diagnostics under single-person execution, so the graded rule is visibly proportionate rather than uniformly heavy.

control_implementations.narrative: A WS-X90 modification currently leaves the platform in a state that is verified only at the next boot, so there is a window between applying a change and confirming the platform is still in a known protection state. The planned change has the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) re-establish the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) measurement chain and confirm it before the modified image is allowed to run operationally, closing that window. The sequence change is designed and not yet fielded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to re-establish and confirm the measurement chain as part of applying a modification, rather than leaving confirmation to the next boot.
Planned to produce the confirmation the controller waits on, so a modified image does not run operationally until its measurement is recorded.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 design documentation in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) is sufficient for the teams that wrote it but not for an independent engineer: several enforcement decisions can only be located by reading source. The planned standard is that the documentation set lets an independent engineer determine, without source access, which component enforces each security decision and what that component does when the decision denies — with the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) session controls as the first section rewritten to that standard. The standard is agreed and the rewrite has not started. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to hold the documentation set at a depth that lets an enforcement decision be located without source access, and to reject a design item that names no enforcing component.
First section planned for rewrite to the standard, since its session controls are the decisions most often traced during assessment.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 depends on two external services: the off-platform archive that receives exported records from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), and the release signing service that populates the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with signed release metadata. The signing service operates under a documented control set with named oversight roles on both sides, and its compliance is reviewed at each release. The log archive is the gap: the service agreement exists but no ongoing monitoring method has been defined, so its control compliance is asserted at onboarding and never re-checked. Defining the quarterly monitoring method for the archive is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Exports records to the external archive; the archive's control compliance is asserted at onboarding and not monitored on an ongoing basis, which is the shortfall for this control.
Receives signed release metadata from the external signing service, whose control set and oversight roles are documented and reviewed at each release.

control_implementations.narrative: The two external services WS-X90 uses were onboarded on engineering judgement without a recorded risk assessment or a named approver. Aurora plans to require a risk assessment before any further security service is acquired or outsourced, and a recorded approval from the program security authority before the service is connected to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) export path or the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) intake. Neither the assessment template nor the approval gate exists yet. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to accept an export destination only where a risk assessment and a recorded approval exist for that service.
Planned to accept signed metadata only from a service whose acquisition carries a recorded approval.

control_implementations.narrative: Providers of all external information systems and services used by WS-X90 are required to declare the functions, ports, protocols and services their service requires. On the wired path this is automated: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) rule set is generated from the declarations and reconciled against the deployed configuration at each release, so an external flow absent from a declaration cannot be permitted. On the tactical link it is not: the provider of the service reached through the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) supplies its waveform service and message set declaration as a document, and reconciliation against the radio's configured service list is a manual pre-deployment step that has been missed once. Automating the radio reconciliation is the open action, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) export destination declaration is folded into the same reconciliation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Rule set is generated from provider declarations and reconciled automatically at each release, so an undeclared external flow cannot be permitted on the wired path.
Its external export destination is covered by the same declaration set, so the archive's required services are declared rather than discovered.
Waveform service and message set declaration is reconciled against the radio's configured service list by hand before deployment; the manual step is the shortfall.

control_implementations.narrative: Aurora's relationships with the WS-X90 external log archive and release signing providers rest on service agreements that state availability and support terms but not the security properties the program actually relies on. The planned change documents, per provider, the trust conditions the relationship depends on — key custody for the signing service, retention and access constraints for the archive — and reviews them when either side changes. The trust statements are drafted and unsigned. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Depends on the signing provider's key custody, which the planned trust statement makes an explicit condition of the relationship rather than an assumption.
Depends on the archive provider's retention and access constraints, which the planned trust statement records and makes reviewable.

control_implementations.narrative: Neither the external log archive receiving Security Log Collector (LRU-018) exports nor the release signing service populating the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) carries a jurisdictional constraint on where processing and storage occur, and neither provider has been asked to state its facility locations. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Export destination carries no jurisdictional constraint; the archive's processing and storage locations are unstated.
Signing service carries no jurisdictional constraint; the facility performing the signing operation is unstated.

control_implementations.narrative: Every WS-X90 software and firmware component is delivered with a detached signature and a manifest entry in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020); the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) verifies the signature against the release key before staging and refuses any image that does not verify, so an unsigned or altered image never reaches a target LRU. Verification is repeated at execution: the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) measures each firmware image at every boot and records the measurement, which detects a modification made after staging and before execution — the window that staging-time verification alone leaves open. Both halves are fielded and exercised at each release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds the manifest entry and detached signature for every delivered software and firmware component, and is the source the staging verification is performed against.
Verifies each image signature against the release key before staging and refuses to stage an image that does not verify, logging the refusal with the image identifier.
Measures each firmware image at every boot and records the measurement, so a modification made between staging and execution is detected before the image is given control.

control_implementations.narrative: The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) reads a supplier-provisioned hardware identity from each LRU at power-on and compares it against the accepted inventory, raising a fault within one power-on cycle for any unit whose identity is absent, unreadable or unmatched; the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) supplies the platform measurement the comparison is anchored to. The check is live for the mission computing and platform management LRUs, whose suppliers fit the identity part. Navigation, timing and payload interface LRUs do not carry it — those suppliers were on contract before the requirement was placed — so for six units the inventory comparison falls back to a serial number read from a maintenance record, which detects a swap only if someone updates the record. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Reads the supplier-provisioned hardware identity at power-on and compares it against the accepted inventory, raising a fault within one power-on cycle on any mismatch.
Supplies the platform measurement the identity comparison is anchored to, so a matched identity on an unmeasured platform is not accepted as valid.

control_implementations.narrative: Change requests against WS-X90 configuration items in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) are today reviewed for engineering impact and schedule; security review happens when the engineer raising the change thinks to ask for it. The planned change makes a recorded security disposition from a named System Security Engineer a required field before a change can be approved for build, with the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) inventory reflecting only changes that carry one. The workflow change is specified and not yet configured in the repository. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to require a recorded security disposition from a named engineer before a change request can move to approved-for-build.
Planned to reflect in the platform inventory only those changes that carry a security disposition, so an undisposed change is visible as an inventory divergence.

control_implementations.narrative: Mission and platform software entering the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) has passed a static analysis run performed on the exact source revision that was built — the pipeline rejects a submission whose analysis run cites a different revision hash, which is what stops a clean scan of an older tree being reused. Every high-severity finding is either fixed before release or carries a recorded engineering disposition naming the reviewer and the reason; the disposition list is reviewed at each release rather than accumulating. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) software is the largest body covered, and the analysis configuration itself is a controlled item so a rule set cannot be quietly narrowed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Rejects a build submission whose static analysis run cites a source revision other than the one built, and holds the analysis configuration as a controlled item.
Hosts the largest analysed body of software; its release is gated on the high-severity finding list being empty or fully dispositioned.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 holds a threat model for each external and payload interface stating the assumed adversary access, the component that mediates it, and the analysis outcome for each identified attack path. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) model is current and was re-run when the external rule generation changed. The payload models are the shortfall: the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) and Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) models are drafted but have not been through review, so their identified attack paths carry no agreed disposition and the interlock's independence claim has not been challenged by anyone outside the design team. Review of both payload models is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Threat model is current and was re-run when the external rule generation changed, with each attack path carrying a disposition.
Threat model drafted covering the command path and its mediation point; not yet reviewed, so attack path dispositions are provisional.
Threat model drafted covering the interlock authorization path; the independence claim has not been challenged outside the design team.

control_implementations.narrative: The WS-X90 mission software toolchain is pinned by version and configuration in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), a build is reproducible from the recorded tool set, and a toolchain change goes through review as a controlled change with its own impact statement; the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) will only run a build from a pinned toolchain record. Payload interface firmware is the exception: it is still built by the supplier on an unpinned vendor toolchain, so those builds are not reproducible on Aurora's side and a tool change there arrives without notice. Bringing the payload firmware build onto a pinned toolchain is on contract and not yet delivered. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds the pinned toolchain versions and configurations as controlled items and records the tool set each build was produced with.
Will only run a build whose repository record cites a pinned toolchain, which is where an unpinned build is caught in ground support.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 has no recorded criticality analysis; component importance is understood informally and is not stated at design reviews. The planned analysis ranks components by the consequence of their failure or subversion at each design review decision point, and places the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011), Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) in the highest tier with the protection measures each tier attracts named explicitly. The rigour is agreed and the first analysis has not been performed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to be placed in the highest criticality tier on the basis that its subversion permits an unauthorised payload action.
Planned to be placed in the highest tier because its subversion undermines every channel and storage protection that depends on its key use.
Planned to be placed in the highest tier because its subversion invalidates the measurement chain the rest of the platform's trust rests on.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 release candidates are not scanned against their declared component inventory for known vulnerabilities before release; vulnerability information reaches the program through the flaw remediation process after fielding. The planned change scans each release candidate against the inventory held with the release in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), assesses exploitation potential in the WS-X90 configuration rather than in the abstract, and delivers the output and proposed mitigations to the Product Security Engineer before release, with the results also exported to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) for trend visibility. Nothing is running yet. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Planned to hold the declared component inventory each release candidate is scanned against, and to gate release on the scan output being delivered.
Planned to receive the scan results so vulnerability trend across releases is visible alongside operational security data.

control_implementations.narrative: Technicians are trained on WS-X90 ground support tooling by Aurora staff using material assembled internally; the suppliers of the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and the ground support tooling provide no training of their own, so the security functions those products expose and their failure behaviour are taught second-hand. The planned change puts supplier-delivered hands-on training on contract, completion of which is a precondition for issuing a maintenance credential usable from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) or the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017). The training requirement is drafted and not placed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Its supplier is planned to deliver hands-on training covering the session security functions it exposes and the behaviour on failure.
Planned to require a maintenance credential that is issued only on recorded completion of the supplier training.
Planned to apply the same credential precondition for provisioning actions, so training completion gates the higher-consequence workflow too.

control_implementations.narrative: The WS-X90 design specification carries a complete allocation table mapping every tailored control to a physical or logical component, and it describes how the mediation points combine — the Mission Computer (LRU-001) service manifest check, the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) boundary decision and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) authorization — into a single protection story rather than three independent ones. The allocation table is complete and reviewed. The composition narrative is not: the section that explains how the payload interface protections combine with the mission computing ones is outstanding, so the architecture currently reads as two well-described halves with an undescribed seam between them, which is where an assessor would expect to find the gap. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Allocation and mediation description complete; its service manifest check is the anchor the composition narrative builds from.
Allocation and mediation description complete, including the boundary decision and its fail-closed path.
Allocated and described individually, but the narrative explaining how its authorization composes with mission computing protections is outstanding.

control_implementations.narrative: Commit and signing authority over WS-X90 mission software and Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) firmware is granted on team membership; the access authorization the role requires is verified once at onboarding and not re-checked when someone moves between roles. The planned change verifies the authorization before signing authority is issued and re-verifies it whenever the role changes, with the authority record held against the developer identity used by the signing service. The verification step is agreed with the supplier and not yet in force. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Its mission software commit and signing authority is planned to be conditioned on a verified, current access authorization for the role.
Its firmware signing authority is planned to carry the same condition, with re-verification on any role change.

control_implementations.narrative: The component inventory held by the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) carries a vendor support end date for hardware and software items, and any item within 12 months of that date is surfaced on the replacement or alternative-support list before support lapses. Dates are populated for mission computing, communications and platform management items. Navigation and timing are the gap: the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and Timing Receiver (LRU-005) entries carry no support end date because the supplier has not stated one, which means the two items with the shortest expected production life are the two the program cannot schedule against. Obtaining the dates is on contract; the technology refresh plan is blocked behind them. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds the component inventory and surfaces any item within 12 months of its vendor support end date on the replacement list.
Inventory entry carries no vendor support end date, so it cannot be scheduled for replacement or alternative support.
Inventory entry carries no vendor support end date; its receiver front end is the item with the shortest expected production life on the platform.

control_implementations.narrative: SC-1 is carried as data rather than as a filing cabinet: the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) stores the WS-X90 system and communications protection policy and its procedures as signed baseline objects with issue date, owner and supersession history, and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) reads that issue date when it assembles a release and refuses to build against a baseline older than 12 months. What is missing is the review itself - the annual reissue is a calendar item held by the security engineering lead, not a workflow with a recorded decision, so the check enforces freshness of the artifact without evidencing that a review took place. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds the SC policy and the implementing procedures as signed baseline objects, keeps the issue date and owner in the object metadata, and retains the superseded revisions so the annual cycle is auditable.
Reads the referenced policy baseline date during provisioning package assembly and blocks the build when it is older than 12 months, recording the block against the release request.

control_implementations.narrative: User-facing mission function and system management function are separated on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) by the partition table in the approved build: mission applications and the platform management agent hold distinct memory-protected partitions with their own scheduling budgets and no shared writable region, and the management-plane socket is not visible from a mission partition. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) binds its service endpoints to the management interface alone, so the separation holds at both ends rather than depending on the caller behaving. Rejections are counted on LRU-001 so an attempt is visible rather than silent. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Runs mission applications and the platform management agent in separate memory-protected partitions with distinct scheduling budgets, and drops any management-plane call originating in a mission partition at the partition boundary before it reaches a socket.
Binds its management service endpoints only to the management interface, so a call that somehow leaves a mission partition still has no listener to reach, and counts every refused bind attempt.

control_implementations.narrative: Security functions are isolated on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) by a dedicated partition whose image and partition table are measured and locked by the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) during authenticated boot, and by delegating all key use to the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) so key material never enters the mission address space. The isolation is asserted at the memory-protection and boot-measurement level. It is not complete: the last-level cache is shared between the security partition and mission workloads with no way partitioning, so a timing side channel between them is not excluded, and the isolation analysis carries that as an open item pending a processor configuration change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Hosts the security enforcement partition with a dedicated scheduling budget and no writable memory shared with mission partitions; all cryptographic operations leave the partition through one mediated interface rather than being performed in place.

Measures the partition table and the security partition image during authenticated boot and locks the configuration registers, so the isolation boundary cannot be changed once mission code is running.
Performs every key operation the security partition needs, which keeps key material out of the Mission Computer address space entirely and makes the isolation boundary meaningful rather than nominal.

control_implementations.narrative: Residual information in shared resources is handled on the release path, not the allocation path: the Mission Computer (LRU-001) fills a shared buffer with the approved pattern as it is released back to the pool, and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) does the same for storage blocks and refuses to issue a block its free-pool metadata does not mark cleared. Placing the clear at release removes the race where a fast consumer reads a block before an allocation-time clear runs. Byte-level comparison after re-issue is part of the build acceptance test rather than a one-off check. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Overwrites a shared buffer with the approved fill pattern when it is released rather than when it is next allocated, so an early read by the next holder cannot observe residue ahead of the clear.
Overwrites a released storage block before returning it to the free pool and refuses to issue a block that its free-pool metadata does not mark as cleared.

control_implementations.narrative: Denial-of-service effects are limited at two points: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) polices each external interface to the approved traffic profile ahead of its session table so a flood is dropped before it consumes session state, and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) applies per-port storm control so an internal flood cannot starve the payload command segment. What is missing is the resource side of the control: LRU-007 does not yet export session-table and buffer occupancy, so the program can show that flooding is shed but cannot show how close the platform came to exhaustion during the event. Consistent with the moderate availability categorization no redundant ingress path exists. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Applies a per-interface ingress rate limit from the approved traffic profile and sheds excess at the policer ahead of the session table, so an established mission session keeps its committed rate while the flood is dropped.
Enforces per-port broadcast and multicast storm control at the profiled thresholds so a flood on one internal segment does not consume switch fabric shared with the payload command segment.

control_implementations.narrative: Restricting the platform's ability to attack other systems is enforced at the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) rather than trusted to the on-platform sender: egress is policed per external destination and matched against the approved flow list, and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) will only transmit what the gateway hands it, so no on-platform process has an independent path off the platform. The gap is the shape of the policer - it counts per destination, so a compromised process that spreads a low-rate flood across many destinations stays under every individual cap. An aggregate egress budget is on the gateway configuration backlog. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Applies a per-destination egress policer and an approved-flow match, dropping traffic that fails either check and counting the drops by originating on-platform partition.
Transmits only frames handed to it by LRU-007 on the approved mission flows, so there is no path from an on-platform process to the radio that bypasses the egress policer.

control_implementations.narrative: Capacity and bandwidth management for WS-X90 is planned, not built. The design intent is a recorded reserve on each Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) segment and a stated link budget and queue behaviour for the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), both sized against the worst-case mission traffic profile and held in the approved configuration baseline so a configuration change that eats the reserve is visible. Because the system is categorized moderate for availability the approach is provisioning and documented degradation, not redundancy: the analysis will say what is lost when a link is lost rather than claim a failover the platform does not have. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Will carry a recorded per-segment bandwidth reserve against the worst-case mission profile, sized so that the payload command segment retains its allocation when every other segment is at peak.
Will carry a recorded link budget and queue depth figure for the worst-case mission profile, with the excess handling behaviour stated rather than left to the radio default.

control_implementations.narrative: Detection and monitoring of denial-of-service indicators runs between two LRUs: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) samples per-interface utilisation, connection-rate and drop counters and exports them every 60 seconds with a sequence number, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) holds the threshold state and raises one alert per sustained excursion instead of one per sample. The gap is on the resource side of the enhancement - LRU-007 does not export session-table or buffer occupancy, so an attack that exhausts state at a low packet rate would not show in the exported set. Adding those counters is scheduled with the next gateway telemetry change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Samples utilisation, connection-rate and drop counters per interface and exports them on a 60-second cadence over the management segment, with a sequence number so a missed export is detectable.
Evaluates the arriving counters against the profiled thresholds, holds the three-interval state, and raises a single alert per excursion rather than one per interval.

control_implementations.narrative: The number of external connections is held at two by construction rather than by policy: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) is the only LRU with an interface in the external address space, carrying the ground data link and the maintenance service port, and every other external-capable interface in the platform hardware is administratively down in the fielded baseline with its state measured at boot. The interface inventory is checked against the baseline as part of configuration verification, so a third connection cannot appear without an approved change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Terminates both external connections and is the only LRU with an interface in the external address space; every other external-facing interface in the hardware is administratively down in the fielded baseline and its state is measured at boot.

control_implementations.narrative: Each external telecommunication service terminates on its own managed interface of the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) under a named traffic-flow policy, with confidentiality and integrity provided on the wire and inbound routing and control-plane protocol traffic filtered before any forwarding decision; the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) presents its link through that same policy and cannot originate traffic outside it. Two parts of the enhancement are open: the outbound publication that would let a remote network detect unauthorized control-plane traffic coming from WS-X90 is not built, and the exception review described in the companion requirement is still manual. This narrative is synthetic demo content. Exceptions to a traffic-flow policy are held as objects in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) rather than as comments in a rule set, each with the mission justification, the duration of the need, an owner and a last-review date, and the review interval is the 180 days that CNSSI 1253 carries for this enhancement. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is designed to refuse a gateway build containing a stale exception but that check is not yet enforcing, so today the interval is kept by a scheduled manual review. Until the check is switched on, an expired exception could reach a build. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Terminates each external telecommunication service on its own managed interface with a named traffic-flow policy, protects the traffic in transit through the cryptographic path, and filters inbound routing and control-plane protocol traffic before it reaches any forwarding decision.

Presents its mission link to the gateway as a managed interface and refuses to originate traffic that has not come through the named policy, so the radio cannot become an unmanaged second termination.

Stores each traffic-flow policy exception as a first-class object carrying the mission justification, the duration of the need, the owner and the last review date, so an exception cannot exist only as a gateway rule comment.
Reads the exception objects when assembling a gateway configuration and is intended to refuse a build containing one past its 180-day review date; that check is designed but not yet enforcing.

control_implementations.narrative: Deny by default is enforced at both boundary layers. Every interface rule set on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and every port and segment rule set on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) ends in a counted deny, in both directions, and the approved flow list is the only thing that opens a path. The counters matter as much as the deny: a dropped packet is attributable to an interface and a direction, which is what makes an unexpected drop investigable rather than invisible. A rule-set review against the baseline is part of configuration verification and looks specifically for permit-any rules. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Ends every interface rule set, inbound and outbound, with a counted deny, so a flow that is not named in the approved set is dropped and the drop is attributable to an interface and a direction.
Applies the same terminating deny per port and per segment, which is what keeps the payload command segment closed to hosts that have no approved flow onto it.

control_implementations.narrative: Split tunnelling is prevented for the one remote-device case WS-X90 has: a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) connected to the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014). The laptop baseline leaves only the maintenance interface enabled during a session, a posture agent enumerates active interfaces at establishment and every 60 seconds, and LRU-014 drops the session within 5 seconds of a report showing a second interface. The weakness is the trust model: the evidence is the endpoint's own report, so an operator with local control of LRU-019 could suppress it. Independent verification from the gateway side is on the maintenance access backlog. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Requires a posture report at session establishment and at 60-second intervals, and drops the session within 5 seconds of a report showing a second active interface, logging the endpoint identity and the reason.
Runs the posture agent that enumerates active interfaces and routes, and holds a baseline that leaves only the maintenance interface enabled while a session is open.

control_implementations.narrative: Traffic bound for networks outside Aurora Defense Systems' control is routed through the authenticated proxy on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007), which terminates and re-originates the session so no on-platform host holds a connection to an untrusted network; exemptions exist only as named entries carrying a reference to the authorizing official's decision.
