The gap is a real one rather than a paperwork one: firmware retrieval over the maintenance service port still uses an unproxied path, so the exemption set in practice is wider than the named list. Moving that retrieval behind the proxy is the remediation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Hosts the authenticated proxy, terminates and re-originates external-bound sessions on the ground data link so no on-platform host talks directly to an untrusted network, and holds the named exemption list with its decision-record references; the maintenance service port bypass is configured and is the open item.

control_implementations.narrative: Outgoing traffic that would threaten an external system is dropped at the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) against the approved egress threat rules, and the gateway resolves the source address to an originating LRU and partition before sending a denial record to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) inside 60 seconds. The auditing half of the enhancement is incomplete: when the traffic originates from a maintenance session the record names the Maintenance Access Gateway rather than the operator behind it, so attribution stops at a device. Carrying the maintenance session identity forward into the gateway record is the fix. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Evaluates outbound traffic against the approved egress threat rules, drops on a match, and resolves the source address to an originating LRU and partition before emitting the record.
Receives and retains the denial records, correlates them by originating LRU and partition, and is the surface where the missing operator attribution shows as a null field.

control_implementations.narrative: Exfiltration prevention on WS-X90 is a type check plus a cryptographic gate: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) classifies each outbound object against the approved mission data type list and blocks anything unmatched, and it refuses to transmit an object that has not been wrapped by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) under the mission key in force, with the key identifier recorded in the wrap. The enhancement also calls for exfiltration testing, and that is where the program is short: one test has been run against the ground data link, there is no recurring cadence, and the maintenance service port has not been tested at all. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Classifies each outbound object against the approved mission data type list and blocks anything unmatched, and refuses to transmit an object that does not carry an LRU-003 wrap.
Wraps each permitted export under the mission key in force and records the key identifier in the wrap, so an export can later be tied to the key epoch it left under.

control_implementations.narrative: Incoming traffic is constrained as pairs rather than as a source list: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) accepts only the named ground control source addresses and only when the destination is one of the LRUs paired to that source, and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) re-checks the same pairing on the internal segment. Doing the check twice means the restriction survives a host that reaches the internal fabric by some other route, which is the case that a boundary-only check misses. Both pair lists are verified against the approved baseline during configuration verification. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Matches inbound traffic against the approved source list at the external interface and rewrites nothing that is not paired to a named destination, so an approved source with a wrong destination is dropped at the boundary rather than inside.
Repeats the pairing check on the internal segment, which means a host that reaches the internal fabric by any other route still cannot deliver to an LRU outside the approved pairing.

control_implementations.narrative: Host-based boundary protection is fielded on the three WS-X90 components that can run it. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) enforce a ruleset derived from their declared flows, and every other LRU appears on an exemption list with the reason - most are fixed-function hardware with no host stack to filter. The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is the gap: the ruleset is deployed but running in log-only mode pending a field trial, so on the one endpoint that leaves the hangar the filter currently observes rather than blocks. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Runs the host filter in enforcing mode with a ruleset derived from the partition flow model, so a mission partition cannot open a socket outside its declared flows even inside the platform.
Runs the host filter in enforcing mode with a ruleset limited to the provisioning transfer paths and the repository interface.
Carries the same ruleset but in log-only mode pending a field trial, so violations on the maintenance endpoint are recorded and not blocked.

control_implementations.narrative: The security tooling - the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) - is separated from the rest of the platform by a management segment on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) with an explicit managed-interface rule set, and LRU-018 binds its services only to that segment so it does not answer on any other. The enhancement asks for physically separate subnetworks, and WS-X90 has a VLAN on shared switch hardware instead: the logical separation holds against a misrouted host but not against a fabric-level compromise of LRU-009. The program has not yet decided between adding a dedicated switch and accepting the difference. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Binds its collection and query services only to the management segment interface and refuses a connection arriving on any other, so a mission-segment host cannot reach the tooling even if the switch rule set were wrong.
Carries the management segment as a VLAN with an explicit managed-interface rule set between it and the mission segments; the shared fabric is what keeps this short of physical separation.

control_implementations.narrative: Unauthorized physical connection at boundary-crossing interfaces is addressed with keyed locks and port blanks rather than with detection: both Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) external terminations are locked under recorded key control, unused Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) ports are physically blanked per the inventory, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) service connector is locked. What is missing is evidence of tampering: the LRU-014 connector has no tamper-evident seal, so a connection made and removed between inspections leaves nothing behind. Seals are specified and on order. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Both external terminations carry keyed port locks whose key control is held in the platform inventory, so an unauthorized cable cannot be seated without the key.
Unused ports are fitted with physical blanks recorded per port in the inventory, which removes the easiest unauthorized internal connection point.
The maintenance service connector carries a keyed lock but no tamper-evident seal, so seating and unseating is not physically evidenced; this is the open item for this enhancement.

control_implementations.narrative: Privileged access to WS-X90 is funnelled: the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) is the only path, it authenticates the operator and mints the session identifier, and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) refuses a privileged session arriving on any other interface. Because the gateway is a dedicated managed interface rather than a jump host on the general network, the access-control decision and the audit record are made in the same place, and every administrative action LRU-013 performs carries the operator identity and session identifier forward. The command stream is recorded at LRU-014 in order with results. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Is the single termination for privileged access, authenticates the operator, mints the session identifier and records the command stream, so privileged activity is auditable at one point rather than per target LRU.
Refuses a privileged session offered on any interface other than the LRU-014 path and stamps the operator identity and session identifier onto every administrative action it performs.

control_implementations.narrative: Fail-secure behaviour on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) is implemented as a latch rather than as a policy: independent watchdogs cover the policy engine and the forwarding path, either one failing drops the data plane inside 2 seconds, and the closed state is written to non-volatile configuration so a power cycle does not reopen the boundary. Restoring service requires an explicit operator action, which is what stops a reboot from being used as a way past a failed policy engine. The failure-mode analysis enumerates the detected failure paths and shows none of them reaching a permissive mode. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Watchdogs the policy engine and the forwarding path independently, drops the data plane within 2 seconds of either failing, and latches the closed state in non-volatile configuration so a power cycle does not silently reopen the boundary.

control_implementations.narrative: Boundary protection is used inside the platform to isolate the mission-critical payload command function. The Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) carries payload command on a dedicated segment with no inter-segment route to mission or management traffic, and the two LRUs on it - the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) - accept command frames only on that interface. The isolation is structural: a compromised mission host has no route onto the segment, so reaching the interlock is not a matter of defeating a check. Route traces from every other LRU are part of the acceptance test. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Carries the payload command segment with no inter-segment route to mission or management, enforced by the terminating deny on the segment's managed interface rather than by address separation alone.
Accepts payload command frames only on its dedicated segment interface and discards a command frame arriving on its telemetry or management interface.
Holds the independent authorization state on the same isolated segment, so an attacker on the mission segment has no path to the interlock at all rather than a path guarded by a check.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 has one planned connection that this enhancement governs - the unclassified ground segment link - and it is not built. The interface exists on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) but is administratively down in the fielded baseline with its state measured at boot, and no boundary protection device has been selected for the path. The plan is to select and accredit the device, place it in the path, and only then enable the interface under an approved configuration change; until then the honest position is that the connection does not exist rather than that it is protected. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds the planned unclassified ground segment interface administratively down in the fielded baseline; enabling it will require both the selected boundary protection device in the path and an approved configuration change.

control_implementations.narrative: No WS-X90 component connects to a public network, and that is enforced in two different ways because the two exposures are different. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) carries no default route at all, so a destination outside the approved external address set is dropped rather than forwarded toward whatever the upstream router would do with it. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), which is where a public connection would most plausibly appear as a convenience, has no enabled interface to a routable network and receives updates only on removable media enrolled in the Configuration Repository. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Terminates only the approved government network paths, holds no default route, and drops traffic for any destination outside the approved external address set rather than forwarding it upward.
Has no enabled interface to a routable public network in the approved baseline; its only ingress path is enrolled removable media, which is what keeps the provisioning chain off the public internet.

control_implementations.narrative: Critical functions are segmented on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) and the segmentation is enforced twice for the payload path: the switch has no route from other subnets onto payload command, and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) independently rejects an arming frame whose ingress subnet is wrong, so a switch misconfiguration alone cannot deliver one. Three of the four intended subnets exist. Platform management and log export still share a subnet, which means a compromised management host sits alongside the log path it would want to reach; splitting them is a scheduled configuration change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Implements the mission, payload command and combined management-and-log-export subnets with managed interfaces between them; splitting management from log export is the outstanding configuration change.
Rejects and counts any arming frame whose ingress subnet is not the payload command subnet, so the segmentation is enforced at the safety-critical end and not only in the switch.

control_implementations.narrative: Confidentiality and integrity in transmission are provided by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), which wraps every outbound frame before it reaches the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) or the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008); both refuse to transmit an unwrapped frame and verify inbound wraps before any parsing happens. There is no unprotected fallback mode: if the crypto interface is unavailable the link stops rather than degrading. Integrity failures are counted and reported so a modified frame is a visible event, not a silent discard. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Performs the encryption and integrity computation for every outbound frame and holds the keys, so neither the gateway nor the radio ever handles unwrapped mission data or key material.
Refuses to transmit a frame that does not carry an LRU-003 wrap and verifies inbound wraps before the frame reaches any parsing logic.
Applies the same refusal on the radio path, so the mission link cannot fall back to an unprotected mode when the crypto interface is unavailable - it stops transmitting instead.

control_implementations.narrative: Pre- and post-transmission handling is where mission data exists in the clear on the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), and the design narrows that window: staging memory is mappable only by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) interface driver, and the transmit buffer is overwritten with the approved fill pattern on release. The receive side is incomplete - inbound staging buffers are reused without an explicit overwrite, so plaintext from a prior frame can persist until it is overwritten by the next one. The fix is a firmware change scheduled against the next radio drop and is tracked as an open gap. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Stages outbound and inbound mission data in a memory region that only the crypto interface driver can map, and overwrites the transmit staging buffer on release; the receive buffer is currently reused without an overwrite.
Is the only consumer permitted to read the staging region, so plaintext exists in the radio only between the staging write and the crypto read rather than across the whole frame lifetime.

control_implementations.narrative: Network disconnect is enforced on the only long-lived session type WS-X90 has. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) tracks per-session inactivity against the 15-minute value CNSSI 1253 carries for this control and terminates at that point, and it deliberately does not treat transport keepalives as activity, so an idle session cannot be held open by a client that is simply still connected. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) drops the transport state at the same time, so the client cannot resume into the old session and must authenticate again. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Tracks per-session inactivity and terminates at 15 minutes, logging the termination with the session identifier and the reason, and does not extend the timer on keepalive traffic that carries no operator action.
Removes the transport state for the terminated session so a client holding the old connection cannot resume into it; a reconnect is a new session and a new authentication.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 does not implement this control. No collaborative computing device or application is fielded on any of the twenty LRUs, but the two ground support endpoints - the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) - expose audio input hardware that the baseline does not disable, and neither gives a physically present user any indication of use. The program has not decided whether to disable the peripherals in the baseline or to tailor the control out on the grounds that no collaborative application exists, and until that decision is recorded no coverage is asserted. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Carries no collaborative computing application in the baseline, but the hardware exposes audio input and the baseline neither disables it nor indicates its use.
Same position: no collaborative computing application in the baseline and no peripheral control or use indication.

control_implementations.narrative: Security attributes travel with navigation data across the internal bus: the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) stamps every forwarded message with a source identifier and its own integrity check result, and the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) refuses a message whose attribute set is missing or unrecognised instead of defaulting it, which is the behaviour that makes the attribute load-bearing. The association breaks at the subsystem edge: when navigation state is exported to mission compute the attributes are dropped, so a consumer there cannot tell a checked value from an unchecked one. Extending the attribute across that interface is the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content. On the payload path the attribute that matters is which command authority was in force. The Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) stamps it into every command frame and discards returning telemetry whose attribute does not match, which is what prevents a stale stream being read as a response to the current authority, and the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) copies the attribute into its health frames. The association is lost at storage: LRU-012's stored telemetry record has no attribute field, so an after-the-fact review cannot tell which authority a stored reading belonged to. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Stamps each forwarded sensor message with a source identifier and the result of its own input integrity check, so downstream consumers see which sensor a value came from and whether it passed.
Refuses to admit a navigation message into the solution when the attribute set is absent or unrecognised, and counts the refusal rather than substituting a default value.

Places the in-force command authority into the attribute field of every command frame and discards a returning telemetry frame whose authority attribute does not match, so a stale or crossed telemetry stream is not attributed to the current authority.
Copies the authority attribute from the command it is responding to into its health frames; it does not yet carry that attribute into the stored telemetry record, which is the gap.

control_implementations.narrative: Integrity verification of transmitted attributes is designed and not yet built. Today the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) act on attribute blocks that travel unprotected alongside the message body, so a modified attribute is accepted at face value. The plan adds a keyed check computed over the attribute block through the shared cryptographic interface, verified before the attribute is used in any admission or authorization decision, with a failed check treated as an absent attribute rather than as a warning. The change is scheduled against a named firmware drop. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Will verify the keyed check over the navigation attribute block before admitting a message to the solution, and will count a failed check as a refusal rather than downgrading it to a warning.
Will verify the same check over the payload authority attribute before treating a telemetry frame as belonging to the current authority.

control_implementations.narrative: Anti-spoofing of the attribute that says a navigation integrity check passed is not implemented. The exposure is specific: today the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) trusts the claim in the attribute, so an injected message asserting a passed check is admitted to the navigation solution on that assertion alone. The design binds the claim to a per-boot value held only by the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006), tagging each attribute so a claim can only come from the component that could have made the check, and rejecting attributes replayed from earlier boots. It is on the navigation firmware plan and carried as an open risk in the meantime. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Will derive a per-boot value at start-up and include a value-derived tag in each attribute it stamps, so a check result cannot be claimed by anything that did not hold the value that boot.
Will reject an attribute whose tag does not match the current boot value, which also rejects an attribute replayed from an earlier boot.

control_implementations.narrative: Cryptographic binding between attributes and the information they describe is planned. Without it, the attribute and the body are two adjacent fields, and a bus participant able to assemble a message can pair a genuine attribute block with a body of its choosing. The design has the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) sign the concatenation of the attribute block and the body and the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) verify it before use. The open engineering question is rate: the analysis to confirm LRU-003 can sustain the per-message signing rate in the worst-case mission profile is part of the planned work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Will compute and verify the binding signature over the concatenated attribute block and body, and holds the key so the binding cannot be produced by a compromised bus participant.
Will reject a message whose binding does not verify, including one assembled from a valid body and a valid attribute block taken from different messages.

control_implementations.narrative: Certificates come from the approved government PKI under the program certificate policy, and the part that gets checked is the trust store: the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) holds the anchors in protected storage and cannot add one at run time, so the store is what was provisioned and nothing else. The Configuration Repository (LRU-020) holds the authoritative anchor list as a signed object with its change history, which makes adding an anchor an approved configuration event with an owner rather than an edit somebody made. Configuration verification compares the two. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds the trust store in protected storage and will not add an anchor at run time; the store contents are set at provisioning and verified against the LRU-020 list during configuration verification.
Holds the authoritative anchor list as a signed object with the full change history, so an anchor addition is an approved, attributable configuration event rather than an edit.

control_implementations.narrative: Mobile code on WS-X90 means interpreted and dynamically loaded content inside load modules, not browser content, and it is governed by a dated acceptable and unacceptable technology list with a named owner. For the Mission Computer (LRU-001) the list has been enforced at build time throughout the assessment - a module containing an unacceptable technology fails the build and the failure names it - which is why the airborne baseline can be asserted. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) tooling pipeline came under the same gate on 2026-11-03, when the existing build scan was extended over it and the software configuration control board reading became a record of the decision rather than the decision itself, so both endpoints now refuse an unacceptable technology by build rather than by reviewer attention. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Load modules are scanned at build time for interpreted and dynamically loaded content and the build fails on a technology outside the acceptable list, so an unacceptable technology cannot reach the airborne baseline.

Provisioning tooling has been scanned by the same build-time check as the airborne baseline since 2026-11-03; a technology outside the acceptable list fails the tooling build, and the control board reading now records that outcome instead of standing in for it.

control_implementations.narrative: Identifying unacceptable code and acting on it is implemented as a flag plus a refusal plus an action: the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) evaluates each package manifest against the unacceptable technology list and flags the package object, the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) refuses a flagged package, and the refusal opens a control board item with an owner so it cannot simply be retried. The limit is that the check reads manifests, not content, so a package that under-declares what it contains passes. Adding content inspection at repository intake is the identified fix. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Evaluates each incoming package manifest against the unacceptable technology list and sets a flag on the package object, which is what LRU-017 reads; it does not inspect package content.
Refuses to provision a flagged package and opens a control board item naming the package, the technology and the owner, so a refusal produces an action rather than a retry.

control_implementations.narrative: Verifying that acquisition, development and use of mobile code meets the category handling rules is planned work. The rules themselves are the ones CNSSI 1253 carries for this enhancement - signed versus unsigned handling, constrained execution, trusted source over an assured channel - and the plan is to make the category a field on the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) acceptance record and to have the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) refuse a package that has none, so the category becomes a gate rather than a label. Today the same judgement is made by a reviewer against development artifacts, with no record that survives into the release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Will gain a category field with an allowed value set on the package acceptance record, and will hold the evidence that the category handling rules - signing, constrained execution, trusted source over an assured channel - were met.
Will refuse to release a package whose acceptance record carries no category, which is what turns the category from a label into a gate.

control_implementations.narrative: Downloading and executing unacceptable code is prevented most firmly where it matters most: the Mission Computer (LRU-001) has no run-time code loader reachable from any interface and executes only signed modules from the measured baseline, so there is nothing on the airborne side for a downloaded module to run in. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) verifies package signatures and blocks failures by default, but an operator override remains available and is only recorded after use, which means an unsigned package can reach the provisioning chain if an operator chooses. Removing that override is the tracked remediation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Executes only signed modules from the measured baseline and has no run-time code loader reachable from any interface, so a downloaded module has nothing to execute it.
Verifies package signatures before download completes and blocks on failure, but exposes an operator override whose use is logged after the fact rather than approved in advance.

control_implementations.narrative: Automatic execution of embedded code is blocked on the two WS-X90 endpoints that handle documents at all - the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) - across the application scope CNSSI 1253 names for this enhancement. A document with an embedded construct opens with it disabled, the policy is set in the approved baseline and is not locally changeable, and enabling a construct is an explicit operator action that produces a record naming the file, the construct and the operator. On LRU-017 the same action also raises a review item if the file is inside a package under assembly, so a provisioning artifact cannot quietly acquire an enabled construct. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Opens document formats with embedded execution disabled by policy that the operator cannot change locally, and emits a log record naming the file, the construct and the operator when an enable action is taken.
Applies the same policy, and because the workstation also assembles provisioning packages the enable action additionally raises a review item on any file inside a package under assembly.

control_implementations.narrative: Secure name resolution from the authoritative source is planned. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) already serves the internal WS-X90 name space and the zone content is under configuration control, but responses carry no origin-authentication or integrity artifact, so the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) accepts them on the basis of where they came from. The planned work selects the artifact format and the key holder, enables signing on LRU-013, and switches LRU-007 to discard unsigned responses at the same time. WS-X90 operates one flat internal zone with no child zones, so the chain-of-trust element of the control has no delegation to cover. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Hosts the authoritative internal zone today and will gain response signing; the zone content is already under configuration control, which is the prerequisite for signing it meaningfully.
Will be configured to discard unsigned internal name responses once signing is live; it currently accepts them because there is nothing to verify.

control_implementations.narrative: The resolver on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) has recursion disabled and exactly one permitted upstream, the internal authoritative service, and discards responses arriving from anywhere else; the Mission Computer (LRU-001) has that resolver as its only configured address with no fallback entry, so a failed resolution fails rather than escaping to another path. What is not implemented is the verification the control asks for: no origin authentication or integrity check is performed on the response, because the authoritative side does not yet produce artifacts to check. The two gaps close together. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Has exactly one configured resolver address - the LRU-007 resolver - and no fallback entry, so a failed resolution fails rather than escaping to another path.
Runs the resolver with recursion disabled and a single permitted upstream, discarding a response from any other source; it does not yet verify a response signature because none is produced.

control_implementations.narrative: Architecture and provisioning for name resolution is planned. Today a single instance on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) holds both the authoritative and resolving roles, which means a resolver-side compromise reaches the zone content. The plan splits them into two instances on separate Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) segments, with the resolver holding no zone and no write path. Fault tolerance is deliberately scoped to the moderate availability categorization: the second instance exists for role separation, and the design record states plainly that losing an instance degrades resolution rather than failing over, so nobody reads redundancy into it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Will host two name service instances with separate configurations and separate zone access, one authoritative and one resolving, so a resolver compromise does not carry authoritative zone write access with it.
Will present the two instances on separate segments so the internal and external role separation is enforced by reachability rather than only by service configuration.

control_implementations.narrative: Session identifiers are invalidated as a positive action rather than left to expire. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) removes the identifier from its active table on operator logout, inactivity timeout and link loss, and pushes the invalidation to the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), which rejects and counts any later message bearing it. Covering link loss matters as much as logout - it is the path where a client-side capture is most plausible - and the counter means a replay attempt shows up rather than simply failing quietly. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Removes the identifier from its active table on all three termination paths and pushes the invalidation to LRU-013 rather than waiting for it to expire, so termination is a positive event.
Rejects and counts any message bearing an invalidated identifier, which is what makes a replayed identifier a detected event rather than an unnoticed failure.

control_implementations.narrative: Session identifiers on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) are generated by the gateway and only by the gateway: a client-supplied identifier is rejected rather than adopted, which removes session fixation as a class rather than mitigating it. Each identifier is at least 128 bits drawn from the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) hardware random source rather than from a software generator on the gateway, so identifier entropy has the same provenance as key material. Uniqueness is checked at acceptance across a large sample rather than assumed from the bit length. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Generates every session identifier itself at establishment and rejects a client-supplied identifier outright, so there is no path by which a caller can choose or influence its own session identifier.
Provides the random source for identifier generation, which means identifier entropy comes from the same hardware source as key material rather than from a software generator on the gateway.

control_implementations.narrative: Protected session establishment is constrained to the allowed certificate authorities by chain validation in the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) against the roots in the fielded store, with the authoritative list held as a signed object in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and compared during configuration verification. The gap is in how wide the allowed set really is: only roots are listed, so any intermediate under an allowed root is accepted, and the intended set is narrower than that. Pinning the specific intermediate authorities is the identified fix and is tracked as an open gap. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Validates the peer chain against the allowed roots and refuses session establishment on a failure; it does not yet hold an explicit intermediate list, which is why any intermediate under an allowed root is currently accepted.
Holds the authoritative allowed-CA list as a signed object and is the source the fielded LRU-003 store is verified against during configuration verification.

control_implementations.narrative: Failing to a known state is enforced by the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002), which drives the Mission Computer (LRU-001) to the defined secure state - interfaces down, keys evicted, nothing partially running - within 5 seconds of a boot integrity failure or a watchdog expiry, and holds it there rather than retrying, so a persistent fault is visible instead of masked. The coverage the control asks for is all failure types on all components, and WS-X90 is short of that: a failure detected inside a running mission partition is handled by that partition's own handler, which may keep other partitions running. Extending LRU-002 coverage to in-partition failure reports is the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content. The state-preservation half of failing to a known state is handled by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016), which writes the failure cause, the last known good configuration identifier and the platform integrity state into the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) before power-down, and by LRU-015 making that record readable through the maintenance procedure without needing a normal boot - which is the case that matters, since the platform that failed may not boot. The blind spot is a failure during a recovery operation: LRU-016 is the writer, so when it is the failing element no record is produced. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Detects boot-time integrity failures and watchdog expiry and drives the platform to the defined secure state, holding it there rather than attempting an automatic retry that would mask a persistent fault.
Brings external interfaces down and evicts loaded keys on entry to the secure state, so the state is defined by what is off rather than by what stopped running.

Writes the failure record - cause, last known good configuration identifier, platform integrity state - on the path into the secure state, ahead of power-down, and identifies the configuration to recover from rather than leaving the choice to the technician.
Retains the failure record in protected storage across power cycles and exposes it to the maintenance read procedure without requiring the platform to boot normally first.

control_implementations.narrative: Information at rest is protected across all of it, which is the scope CNSSI 1253 directs for this enhancement: the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) encrypts and integrity-protects every stored object with no exempt type, refusing rather than returning a block that fails its check, and the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) holds the keys so removed media is unreadable even with a compatible reader. Recovery images written by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) go through the same path, so the objects most valuable to someone holding removed media are not the exception the inventory forgot. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Encrypts and integrity-protects every stored object with no exempt object type, and refuses to return a block whose integrity check fails rather than returning it with a warning.
Holds the storage keys so the media and the keys are never co-located; media removed from the platform cannot be read even with a compatible reader.
Writes recovery images through the same protected path, so the recovery material - the objects most useful to an attacker holding removed media - is not an exception.

control_implementations.narrative: Key storage is hardware-protected and is the only place keys exist: the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) holds every WS-X90 key in its hardware key store and exposes operations rather than material, so other LRUs work with handles and never receive key bytes. The fielded command set has no plaintext export path at all, including under maintenance authority, which is the case that most often reintroduces one. The key inventory is reconciled against the store slots during configuration verification so a key that exists outside the store would show up as an unmatched inventory entry. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Holds every platform key in the hardware key store, exposes operations rather than key material, and has no fielded command that returns plaintext key bytes; other LRUs use keys by handle and never receive a copy.

control_implementations.narrative: Operations security for WS-X90 is an intent in the program plan rather than a practice. The exposure it is meant to address is concrete - Configuration Repository (LRU-020) release metadata names components, interfaces and baseline structure, and Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) exports carry the same information in a form that leaves program control easily - but no criteria, reviewer role or decision record exist, so nothing is reviewed today and nothing records that. The planned work defines the artifact types in scope, the criteria and the reviewer role, and schedules a first review against a named release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Release metadata - component names, interface identifiers, baseline structure - is the artifact most likely to leave program control, and will be the first review target once criteria exist.
Printed and exported provisioning artifacts are the second review target; today they leave with no review step and no record that one occurred.

control_implementations.narrative: Port and I/O device access on the airborne components is closed in firmware rather than at the operating system, and the settings are covered by the boot measurement, so re-enabling a port on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) is a configuration change that shows up rather than a local action that does not. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) is closed the same way for storage and console, but its debug port is gated by a hardware jumper that sits outside the measured configuration - anyone with physical access and no configuration authority can move it. Replacing the jumper gate with a firmware setting is the tracked remediation. This narrative is synthetic demo content. On the two ground support endpoints the exposure is removable media and wireless, and wireless is handled decisively: the hardware is removed from both the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) rather than disabled in software. Removable media is handled asymmetrically. LRU-017 accepts only media enrolled in the platform inventory and records refusals, which protects the provisioning chain. LRU-019 accepts any media presented to it, which means the endpoint that travels is the one without the check. Deploying the enrolment check on LRU-019 is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: External storage, debug and console ports are disabled in firmware settings that are measured at boot, so re-enabling one is a configuration change that shows in the measurement rather than a local action.
Storage and console ports are disabled in firmware, but the debug port is gated by a hardware jumper that is outside the measured configuration; this is the open item.

Wireless hardware is removed and the single provisioning media port accepts only enrolled media, refusing and recording anything else, which is what keeps unenrolled media out of the provisioning chain.
Wireless hardware is removed, but the media port accepts any device presented; the enrolment check is specified and not yet deployed, so the maintenance endpoint is the weaker of the two.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 runs one platform time reference, derived and distributed by the Timing Receiver (LRU-005), and every LRU that timestamps anything disciplines to it - the Mission Computer (LRU-001) for mission and security records, the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) for payload health readings. The tolerance that matters is cross-LRU ordering rather than absolute accuracy, so the acceptance criterion is a 50 ms bound against the reference held across a four-hour run plus a demonstration that records from two LRUs order correctly. The timestamping inventory is checked so no LRU quietly stamps from a free-running local clock. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Derives and distributes the single platform time reference and reports its own synchronisation state, so consumers can tell a distributed reference from a free-running one.
Disciplines its clock to the LRU-005 reference and stamps mission and security records from that disciplined clock rather than from a local counter.
Disciplines its clock to the same reference so payload health readings can be ordered against mission and security records from other LRUs.

control_implementations.narrative: The Timing Receiver (LRU-005) compares its internal clock against the authoritative external source every 60 seconds, logs each comparison with the measured difference, and steps or slews the platform reference when the difference exceeds one second, recording before and after values so a correction is auditable rather than silent. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004) marks solutions computed while LRU-005 reports holdover. The gap is that the mark stays internal to LRU-004: the navigation output message carries no holdover indication, so a downstream consumer cannot tell a holdover solution from a synchronised one. This narrative is synthetic demo content. The value of comparing clocks to an authoritative source shows up in the audit trail, and that is where WS-X90 is partly short. Audit records stored on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and forwarded to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) carry timestamps from the disciplined platform reference rather than local counters, so records from different LRUs correlate within the 50 ms distribution tolerance. What the record format lacks is a synchronisation flag: nothing in a stored record says whether the reference was disciplined or in holdover when it was written, so a correlation across a holdover window cannot be weighted accordingly. Adding the flag is an audit record format change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Compares against the authoritative source on a 60-second cadence, logs each comparison with the measured difference, and corrects the platform reference when the difference exceeds 1 second, recording before and after values.
Marks navigation solutions computed while LRU-005 reports holdover, so a solution built on a drifting reference is distinguishable internally; the mark is not yet carried in the output message.
Stamps each stored audit record from the disciplined platform reference rather than from a local counter, which is what lets stored records from different LRUs be correlated after the fact.
Correlates forwarded records across LRUs on the platform reference timestamp; without the synchronisation flag it cannot weight a correlation by whether the clock was disciplined at the time.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 does not implement this control. Command and control runs over one path - the ground data link terminating on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007), carried by the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) - with no alternate bearer configured on either, so losing the bearer suspends command and control rather than switching it. The system is categorized moderate for availability and no alternate path has been funded or designed; the program owes a recorded decision on whether the mission profile needs one. Until that decision and the build behind it, the honest position is no coverage rather than partial coverage. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Terminates the single command and control path; there is no second termination and no configuration for one.
Carries that path and has no alternate bearer configured, so a bearer loss is a command and control loss rather than a switch.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 carries an SI policy issued at system level, plus an implementing procedure set, both signed and held as controlled documents in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020); the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) release manifest cites the approved policy version so a fielded image can be traced to the policy edition it was built under. The review cadence is set at least annually against the CNSSI 1253 national security system parameter, and an accountable official is named in the procedure set. What is missing is the event-driven half: the procedures do not yet define the specific events, beyond the annual date, that force a reissue, and the SI procedures for the enhancements added by the expanded control set (SI-4 monitoring enhancements and the SI-7 boot integrity enhancements) are still drafts rather than issued documents. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Configuration Repository holds the signed SI policy and procedure set as controlled documents, each with a version identifier, approval date and accountable official; it is the authoritative copy the annual review updates.

Provisioning Workstation records the approved SI policy version identifier in each release manifest it builds, so an image issued to the field is traceable to the policy edition in force when it was produced.

control_implementations.narrative: The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) runs a scheduled inventory sweep that polls every WS-X90 LRU for its installed software and firmware version and compares each answer against the approved release manifest published by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016). The sweep runs at least quarterly, the cadence CNSSI 1253 sets for national security systems, and needs no technician present: results are written into the platform inventory record and any component behind the manifest on a security-relevant update is flagged as a deviation. The comparison is manifest-driven rather than signature-driven, so adding a new LRU to the manifest brings it into scope automatically. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Platform Management Controller schedules and executes the quarterly version poll across all 20 LRUs, performs the manifest comparison and writes the deviation list into the platform inventory record.
Update & Recovery Controller publishes the approved release manifest that defines the expected software and firmware version per LRU, and is the source the sweep compares against.

control_implementations.narrative: The program intends to time-stamp both ends of every security-relevant flaw: identification, taken from the advisory or defect record, and closure, taken from the acceptance of the corrective build into the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). Elapsed interval per severity band will be published against a program benchmark in the monthly status export produced by the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013). Today neither the identification timestamp nor the benchmark set is defined in the defect workflow, so no interval can be computed; the build is scheduled after the SI-2 procedure reissue. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Configuration Repository will supply the corrective-build acceptance timestamp that closes the remediation interval for each flaw, taken from the signed release record.
Platform Management Controller will compile the per-severity interval statistics into the monthly status export and list any flaw that has exceeded its benchmark.

control_implementations.narrative: Security patches for WS-X90 are assembled by the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) pipeline into a single signed bundle whose manifest enumerates every component it touches; the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) verifies that manifest against the pipeline build record and refuses a bundle whose component list is incomplete, so a technician performs one authenticated action per maintenance visit instead of per-LRU manual installation. The gap is coverage: the pipeline currently builds bundles for the mission computing and platform management LRUs only. Navigation, communications and payload interface firmware are still packaged and applied individually, and bringing them into the bundle is the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Update & Recovery Controller validates the bundle manifest against the pipeline build record, refuses incomplete bundles, and applies the accepted bundle across its targeted LRUs from a single technician action.

Provisioning Workstation runs the patch pipeline that assembles and signs the bundle and produces the build record; its current pipeline covers mission computing and platform management components only.

control_implementations.narrative: Superseded images are not left on the platform. After an update is accepted and the platform completes one successful mission-ready cycle on the new version, the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) issues an erase for every upgraded or replaced software and firmware component no longer required for operation — the CNSSI 1253 scope for this enhancement — against the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015). Exactly one prior recovery image per LRU is retained so a controlled rollback remains possible under A=moderate; every other superseded slot is erased and the action is recorded with component id and retired version string. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Update & Recovery Controller decides which images are superseded after a successful mission-ready cycle, issues the erase, and keeps the single retained rollback image per LRU.
Secure Storage Module performs the erase of the retired image regions and holds the retained rollback image; it records the disposal with component id and retired version.

control_implementations.narrative: The design routes any object quarantined by the platform malicious-code checks from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) to an offline analysis enclave on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), with the resulting behaviour report attached both to the incident record and to the flaw-remediation item before that item can be closed. Nothing of this is built: the enclave is specified but not stood up, and the quarantine export path from the collector does not yet exist, so today a quarantined object is held and dispositioned by hand. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Security Log Collector will hold quarantined objects and export them to the offline enclave, and will carry the returned behaviour report back onto the incident record.
Provisioning Workstation will host the offline analysis enclave that characterises quarantined code and produces the behaviour report; the enclave is specified but not yet stood up.

control_implementations.narrative: Detection output no longer lives in per-sensor consoles: the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) registers each platform detection source and presents one merged view, and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) forwards its network detections into that view rather than holding them locally. Sensor liveness is tracked, and a source silent for more than 15 minutes is shown as unavailable. What is missing is completeness of registration — host sensors on the payload and navigation LRUs are not yet registered, so the merged view is authoritative for the network and mission computing paths only, and an operator must still consult those LRUs directly. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Security Log Collector is the registration point and correlation engine for the merged detection view, and tracks per-sensor liveness with the 15-minute unavailability threshold.
Protected Network Gateway runs the network intrusion detection function at the external boundary and forwards its detections into the merged view instead of maintaining a separate console.

control_implementations.narrative: The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) applies its detection rule set to events as they arrive rather than on an operator-driven schedule, with a target of 60 seconds from receipt to rule evaluation and a queue-depth alarm at 5,000 unanalysed events so a backlog is visible rather than silent. The analysis engine and the alarm are in place; automated enrichment — resolving a raw event to the account, LRU and maintenance-session context that makes it actionable — is not, so an analyst still performs that lookup by hand. Consistent with A=moderate, the collector is a single instance and a collector outage suspends near-real-time analysis until it is restored. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Security Log Collector evaluates newly received events against the loaded rule set within the 60-second target, maintains the unanalysed-event queue and raises the 5,000-event depth alarm; enrichment against account and session context is not yet automated.

control_implementations.narrative: Inbound and outbound traffic is watched continuously — the CNSSI 1253 frequency for this enhancement — at all three points where WS-X90 traffic crosses a boundary. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) applies the approved flow policy at the external interface, the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) applies it to mission data communications, and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) applies it between internal segments. The criteria are the flow policy's own tuples, so a flow with an unexpected source, destination, protocol or direction raises a security event whether or not it is correctly encrypted; encryption suppresses content inspection, not flow evaluation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Protected Network Gateway evaluates every external flow against the approved policy continuously and emits the security event for source, destination, protocol or direction violations.
Tactical Data Radio applies the same flow policy to mission data communications it originates and terminates, so radio-borne traffic is evaluated on the same criteria as wireline traffic.
Internal Ethernet Switch enforces and reports on inter-segment flows, catching internal traffic that never reaches the external gateway.

control_implementations.narrative: The program maintains an approved compromise-indicator list — repeated authentication failure on a maintenance port, an unexpected boot measurement reported by the Secure Boot Controller, and a flow policy violation. When the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) matches one, it pushes an alert onto the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) operator panel within 60 seconds and the alert persists across a panel refresh and a controller restart until an operator acknowledges it, with the acknowledging account and time recorded. Alerting is push from the collector, so it does not depend on an operator opening a view. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Security Log Collector matches received events against the approved compromise-indicator list and pushes the resulting alert with the indicator identifier and triggering component.
Platform Management Controller renders the alert on the operator panel, holds it un-dismissed until acknowledged, and records the acknowledging account and timestamp.

control_implementations.narrative: Approved external sessions are terminated at the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) so their content is available to the platform monitoring path inside the gateway boundary, with session keys created and held in the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and never written to gateway persistent storage. The gap is scope: only the management and telemetry session classes are terminated for inspection today. Mission data sessions carried over the Tactical Data Radio remain opaque to monitoring end to end, and the decision on whether to terminate them or to accept flow-level visibility only is still open with the authorising official. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Protected Network Gateway terminates the approved session classes, presents decrypted content to the monitoring path within its boundary and holds no plaintext session content on persistent storage.
Cryptographic Services Module generates and holds the session keys used for the terminated sessions, so key material is not exposed on the gateway even while content is inspected.

control_implementations.narrative: Outbound traffic is profiled per declared mission phase at both external interfaces — the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) — on volume, destination set and periodicity, with an anomaly event raised when observed volume exceeds the phase envelope by more than 25 percent over a rolling five-minute window. Profiles exist for the two most-flown mission phases; the remaining phases run against a permissive default envelope, which is the current limitation, and interior-point analysis on the internal segments has not been built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Protected Network Gateway maintains the per-phase outbound profile at the external interface and raises the volume and new-destination anomaly events.
Tactical Data Radio profiles the outbound mission data it transmits per phase; profiles are populated for two mission phases and default to a permissive envelope otherwise.

control_implementations.narrative: Three activity classes raise an alert with no operator query: privileged account creation, security configuration change outside an approved maintenance window, and interruption of audit forwarding beyond five minutes. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) detects them and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) presents them. The mechanism is automated end to end for these three; the trigger set itself is the shortfall, since the activity classes introduced by the expanded control set — indicator-of-compromise matches and integrity re-verification failures on navigation and timing software — are detected but not yet promoted to automated alert. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Security Log Collector evaluates the three approved trigger classes and generates the alert automatically, carrying the triggering account or component identifier.
Platform Management Controller receives and presents the automated alerts, and correlates a configuration-change alert to the maintenance window record that should have covered it.

control_implementations.narrative: The intent is to use the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) receive chain, which already surveys its assigned bands, as the sensing element for rogue-emitter detection inside the WS-X90 physical envelope, reporting each observation with time, band and signal strength to the platform monitoring path. The observation record format and the monitoring ingest route are specified in the design; the radio firmware change that emits observations, and the detection logic that distinguishes an unexpected emitter from an expected one, are not built. No wireless intrusion detection capability is fielded today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Tactical Data Radio will report emitter observations in its assigned bands with time, band and signal strength; the firmware change and the rogue-emitter detection logic are not yet built.

control_implementations.narrative: WS-X90 has no inspection point on the path where traffic crosses from the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) onto the wireline segment served by the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009). Radio-originated traffic is flow-evaluated at the radio and again at the switch, but the wireline detection rule set is not applied at the crossing itself, so a flow that satisfies both flow policies is not content-inspected on entry to the internal network. No design change has been approved and no work is scheduled; the exposure is recorded rather than described as partial coverage. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Tactical Data Radio is the wireless side of the crossing; it applies flow policy but does not run the wireline detection rule set on traffic it hands off.
Internal Ethernet Switch receives radio-originated traffic onto the wireline segment with no inspection point applying the wireline rule set at the transition.

control_implementations.narrative: The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) correlates three source classes — platform host events, network detections and maintenance-session records — into one ordered timeline. Ordering is only as good as the clocks, so entries are stamped against the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) trusted time source and any contributing source whose offset from it exceeds one second is flagged in the correlation view, which makes a skewed source visible instead of quietly mis-ordering the timeline. Each correlated entry records which time source stamped it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Security Log Collector performs the correlation across host, network and maintenance-session sources and renders the single ordered timeline with per-source skew flags.
Timing Receiver provides the trusted time reference the correlation is stamped against and against which contributing-source clock offset is measured.

control_implementations.narrative: Where the program designates a maintainer as posing elevated risk, the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) is to place that individual's sessions into an enhanced-recording mode capturing full command transcripts from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) — a gateway-side setting, deliberately not a laptop-side one, so it cannot be evaded by using a different endpoint. The gateway already records privileged sessions; what does not exist is the per-individual designation attribute, the authorisation and withdrawal procedure behind it, and the review interval. Until those are written, no enhanced-recording designation can be applied. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Maintenance Access Gateway will hold the elevated-risk designation as a session attribute and switch to enhanced recording for the designated individual's sessions.
Maintenance Laptop is the endpoint whose command traffic is transcribed; the designation is enforced at the gateway so the recording follows the individual, not the device.

control_implementations.narrative: Privileged sessions opened through the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) are transcribed at command level and forwarded to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which holds privileged-session transcripts in a retention class separate from routine platform audit so they are not aged out with ordinary records. What is not yet working is the out-of-window alert: the collector receives the transcript but the approved maintenance-window schedule is not machine-readable to it, so a session opened outside a window is currently detected on review rather than raised at the time. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Maintenance Access Gateway captures the command-level transcript of every privileged session it brokers and forwards it as the session proceeds.
Maintenance Laptop is the authorised endpoint whose privileged commands are captured; it holds no local copy of the transcript.
Security Log Collector retains privileged-session transcripts in their own retention class; it cannot yet evaluate them against the approved maintenance-window schedule.

control_implementations.narrative: Both network enforcement points compare what they observe against the approved WS-X90 service baseline at least daily: the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) for internal segment services, and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) for services reachable at the external interface. A listening service that is not on the baseline is both written to audit and alerted, and the check is service-level rather than host-level, so an unauthorised service offered by an otherwise authorised LRU is caught. Removal of an approved service produces no alert, keeping the signal specific to unauthorised additions. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Internal Ethernet Switch observes listening services and open ports on the internal segments and performs the daily comparison against the approved service baseline.
Protected Network Gateway performs the same comparison for services reachable across the external interface and raises the alert alongside the audit record.

control_implementations.narrative: Host-level sensors run on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), reporting process start, privileged operation and configuration-file change to the platform monitoring path. Both sensors are signed elements of the approved baseline, so a maintenance session cannot stop or remove them without breaking the baseline measurement. Coverage stops there: the Update & Recovery Controller and the Secure Storage Module carry no host sensor, which leaves the update and storage paths visible only through their own event streams. Extending the sensor to those LRUs is the outstanding work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Mission Computer runs the host sensor covering process start, privileged operation and configuration-file change for the mission software domain, as a signed baseline element.
Platform Management Controller runs the same sensor over platform administrative services; its sensor cannot be stopped from an authenticated maintenance session.

control_implementations.narrative: Indicators of compromise from the program's approved threat sources are to be held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) as versioned, signed indicator sets with source attribution, then distributed into the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) detection rules with the loaded version visible in the monitoring view. The repository can hold the artifacts today, but no indicator source is under agreement, no set has been ingested, and the repository-to-collector distribution path is unbuilt, so no indicator-driven detection is running. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Configuration Repository will hold versioned, signed indicator sets with source attribution as the authoritative program copy.
Security Log Collector will load the distributed indicator set into its detection rules and display the active set version in the monitoring view.

control_implementations.narrative: Monitoring visibility is taken from the network rather than from the hosts. The Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) mirrors traffic at the mission and maintenance segment boundaries and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) mirrors at the external interface, with mirror destinations restricted to the monitoring path in both configurations, so a host with no local sensor is still observed. The shortfall is at the payload boundary: traffic between the Payload Interface Controller and the mission computing segment is not mirrored, leaving that key internal interface visible only through endpoint reporting. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Internal Ethernet Switch provides mirrored visibility at the mission and maintenance segment boundaries with mirror destinations restricted to the monitoring path.
Protected Network Gateway provides the same mirrored visibility at the external interface so external traffic is observable independently of host cooperation.

control_implementations.narrative: The plan is to publish each accepted security alert and advisory as a machine-readable record in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) — identifier, affected-component list, action class — and push it to an advisory view on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), removing the manual mail distribution step and letting an advisory be linked to the flaw-remediation item it drives. The record schema is drafted; the repository publication step and the collector advisory view are not built, and advisories are distributed by hand today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Configuration Repository will publish accepted advisories as machine-readable, versioned records carrying affected components and an action class.
Security Log Collector will present the advisory view to engineering and maintenance staff and link advisories to the corresponding flaw-remediation items.

control_implementations.narrative: Security function verification runs in two independent places. On the mission computing chain, the Mission Computer (LRU-001) self-tests access decision, audit record generation and cryptographic service availability from the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) at power-on, at transition into mission-ready state and on privileged command, taking the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) reported platform state as a precondition; a failed test blocks the mission-ready transition. On the payload side, the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) verifies its own authorization and interlock logic before every arming sequence and reports the result through the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012). In both cases the anomaly action is to hold — restricted state on the mission side, safe state on the payload side — rather than to restart or shut down, which suits an A=moderate system, and the alert goes to the system/security administrator at a minimum, the CNSSI 1253 recipient for this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Mission Computer executes the security function self-test at the three defined triggers and refuses the mission-ready transition when any element of the test fails.
Secure Boot Controller supplies the measured platform state that is the precondition for the self-test, so a verification pass on a mismeasured platform is not possible.
Cryptographic Services Module is exercised as part of the self-test; its failure to answer a service request is one of the three verified conditions.
Payload Safety Interlock verifies its authorization and state-interlock logic before each arming sequence and holds the safe state on failure rather than restarting the payload interface.
Payload Telemetry Unit carries the interlock verification result and the failure alert off the payload interface to the operator and monitoring paths.

control_implementations.narrative: The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) compiles security function verification results into a periodic report and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) exports it to responsible security personnel — the CNSSI 1253 recipient set of authorising official, CISO/SAISO or equivalent, ISSO and ISSM. The report exists and is going out. What is incomplete is its content: failed verifications are listed but the disposition of each is entered by hand after the fact rather than drawn from the incident record, so a report can go out with a failure whose action is still blank. Wiring the disposition field to the incident record is open. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Platform Management Controller aggregates verification results across the platform and builds the periodic report, including the list of failed verifications.
Security Log Collector holds the recipient definition and performs the export to the responsible security personnel, so distribution is not dependent on an individual's mail rules.

control_implementations.narrative: Integrity checking runs at two cadences on two parts of the platform. At every startup the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) measures the Mission Computer (LRU-001) boot loader, kernel and signed application set and compares each measurement against the approved release manifest, refusing the mission-ready transition on any mismatch and naming the failing measurement slot. Separately, the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) re-verify their loaded navigation and timing software against stored reference digests at startup and at least every 24 hours of continuous operation, reporting a failure to the platform monitoring path within 60 seconds without interrupting navigation output on a passing check. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Secure Boot Controller performs the startup measurement of the mission software set and holds the comparison against the approved release manifest.
Mission Computer is the measured subject — loader, kernel and signed application set — and is held out of mission-ready state until the comparison passes.
Navigation Processor re-verifies its navigation software against stored reference digests at startup and on the 24-hour operating cadence.
Timing Receiver applies the same re-verification to its timing software and holdover logic, and reports failures on the same 60-second path.

control_implementations.narrative: An integrity discrepancy is not left to be discovered on review. The Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) emits a discrete integrity-violation event naming the failing measurement slot the moment a comparison fails, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) matches that event class to the on-call security engineer notification route, delivering within five minutes with no operator poll. The notification is retained by the collector, so a platform restart after the violation does not erase the fact that it occurred. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

by_component.description: Secure Boot Controller generates the integrity-violation event with the failing measurement slot identifier and the expected and observed values.
Security Log Collector maps the integrity-violation event class to the on-call notification route, delivers it automatically, and retains it across a platform restart.

control_implementations.narrative: On an integrity violation in the mission software set, the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) automatically places the platform in a restricted state that permits only maintenance and recovery functions — the deliberate choice for an A=moderate system, where holding is preferable to an automatic reimage — and the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) offers the last known-good signed image for a technician-authorised recovery. The automatic response is limited to violations in the mission software set: a violation detected in navigation, timing or payload firmware is alerted but does not currently drive the restricted state, and extending the automatic response to those measurement domains is outstanding. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
